clue.text: Slightly mistimed call after break in fighting

definitions.meaning: out by a few seconds, a phrase read literally
the referee's cry ordering the boxers' helpers from the ring before a new round

explanation.surface: A boxing referee calls the restart a fraction late after the interval.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes the phrase literally: a clock or call that is wrong by mere seconds. The second is the boxing call clearing the ring of seconds, the boxers' corner helpers.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, wrong by a few ticks of the clock; idiomatically, the boxing cry at the end of an interval between rounds.

clue.text: Arrest for completion of sentence, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to halt, bring to a standstill
a full point ending a sentence

explanation.surface: Being detained once a prison term is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sentence' suggests prison, but it is the grammatical kind, ended by a full stop.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt something, and the punctuation mark (the full point) that ends a written sentence.

clue.text: Writer Jane gave orders, to

parts.note: Jane Austen created a pompous clergyman in Pride and Prejudice, so as author she gave him holy orders

explanation.surface: An author named Jane bossed someone about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gave orders' reads as bossing, but means ordaining: Austen made her character a clergyman. His name is also the word for a thank-you letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The obsequious rector in Pride and Prejudice, ordained by his creator, Austen.

clue.text: Love to join action? Certainly not!

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, so nil or nought

explanation.surface: A romantic proposal is firmly rejected.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial flat refusal, like 'no way'.

clue.text: Gave a plucky performance?

parts.note: plucky read as plucking strings, so the playing of a guitar or similar

explanation.surface: Someone performed bravely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucky' means brave in the surface, but here it means done by plucking strings.
explanation.definitionFit: Played a stringed instrument casually by sweeping the fingers across the strings.

clue.text: Create disorder Micawber hoped for

definitions.meaning: to turn upside down, throw into confusion
Dickens's Mr Micawber was always waiting for something to turn up

explanation.surface: A Dickens character longed for chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield is forever hopeful that 'something will turn up', so a change for the better is what he wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to overturn or disturb; as a noun, an improvement in fortune, which the ever-optimistic Micawber awaited.

clue.text: Promise there from the beginning, said St John

definitions.meaning: to give one's pledge, as in 'I give you my ...'

definitions.text: there from the beginning, said St John
definitions.meaning: the Gospel of John opens 'In the beginning was the ...'

explanation.surface: A gospel writer insists a pledge has existed since the very start.
explanation.walkthrough: St John's Gospel opens 'In the beginning was the Word', so the second half is a Bible quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: A pledge is one's word of honour; the Gospel of John names the divine Logos as present at creation.

clue.text: Friend's so-called prophetic book

definitions.meaning: an old nickname for a Quaker, a member of the Society of Friends
the shortest book of the Old Testament prophets

explanation.surface: A book of prophecy said to belong to a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: A Friend, capitalised, is a Quaker, and this Old Testament name was a nickname for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Formerly a jocular name for a Quaker, and a minor-prophet book in the Old Testament.

clue.text: Inactive landlord's law not enforced

parts.note: dead means not functioning or inactive

explanation.surface: An idle property owner's rule that nobody upholds.
explanation.definitionFit: A statute or rule still on the books but no longer applied or obeyed.

clue.text: Remove all trace of the sort of rite a religious goes about

indicators.note: goes about means surrounds, so the religious person's word wraps round the rearranged letters

parts.note: a religious, as a noun, is a monk or nun; an oblate is a person dedicated to monastic life

indicators.note: the sort of rite a means some loose rearrangement of those letters

explanation.surface: A monk performs some kind of ritual that erases every sign of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the sort of' makes ITERA from RITE A, and 'goes about' puts it inside OBLATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate is to wipe out or efface completely, leaving no mark behind.

clue.text: One may be running round garden, laughing

definitions.text: One may be running round garden
definitions.meaning: a sunken fence or ditch bounding a park, invisible from the house
the written sound of laughter

explanation.surface: Someone jogs round a garden, giggling.
explanation.walkthrough: A ha-ha is a ditch with a wall sunk in it, used round British country-house gardens to keep livestock out without spoiling the view. 'Running' means extending, not jogging.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape feature: a concealed boundary ditch; also the conventional spelling of a laugh.

clue.text: Question initially this author's nom de plume

definitions.text: Question initially this author's nom de plume

parts.words: Question initially this author's nom de plume
parts.note: the opening letter of question was the single-letter pen name of a Cornish writer and anthologist

explanation.surface: A query's first letter is the pen name of some writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch, editor of the Oxford Book of English Verse, wrote under the pen name 'Q', the first letter of 'Question'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish man of letters who edited the Oxford Book of English Verse signed himself with one letter.

clue.text: Antipodean type of fruit plant

definitions.meaning: a New Zealander, in informal usage
the Chinese gooseberry vine and its furry green fruit

explanation.surface: An Australasian variety of fruit-bearing plant.
explanation.walkthrough: The flightless national bird of New Zealand gives its nickname to New Zealanders, and the fruit was renamed after it for export.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal name for a New Zealander, and also the climbing vine producing furry brown gooseberry-like fruit.

clue.text: Lively as third part of Holst's suite

definitions.meaning: volatile, quick-changing in mood

definitions.text: as third part of Holst's suite
definitions.meaning: like the third movement of The Planets, which depicts the winged messenger planet

explanation.surface: A movement in a Holst orchestral suite is spirited.
explanation.walkthrough: The third movement of Holst's suite The Planets is 'Mercury, the Winged Messenger', so the adjective means 'like that planet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick and changeable in temperament, and also pertaining to the planet portrayed in The Planets' third movement.

clue.text: Shared gift in a way that's prudent

indicators.note: in a way says the letters of shared gift are reshaped into another form

explanation.surface: A gift that was split up in some fashion shows wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Wise in planning ahead and judging future needs, so careful and sensible.

clue.text: Receiver of property possibly sees gain in it

indicators.note: possibly says the following letters are only one possible arrangement, so they are shuffled

explanation.surface: Someone inheriting an estate may see a profit in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text has 'sets', but the page prints 'sees'. 'possibly' rearranges SEES GAIN; 'in it' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, the person to whom rights or an estate are transferred is the transferee or grantee.

clue.text: Something tediously familiar for veteran bowler, perhaps

definitions.meaning: stale, out of date, seen before
an aged hat, a bowler being a kind of hard round hat

explanation.surface: A tired routine from an ageing cricketer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' suggests cricket, but it is the hard felt hat; an elderly one is an old one.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for stale, unoriginal material, and literally an aged piece of headwear such as a bowler.

clue.text: Increase urgency where 'presidents dominate the scene

definitions.meaning: hurry further, go faster
the South Dakota mountain carved with the faces of four US presidents

explanation.surface: Things get more pressing where heads of state are in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: Mount Rushmore, South Dakota, has four presidents' heads carved into it, so they literally dominate the landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurry more, read as a phrase; and the mountain monument bearing giant carved presidential faces.

clue.text: Escort arranged for part of front

indicators.note: arranged means the letters of escort are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A military guard is organised for a stretch of the battle line.
explanation.definitionFit: A section of a battle front or military zone is a division of territory under one command.

clue.text: Result of crop sailors harvested

parts.note: cut down, as with a crop

explanation.surface: Seamen gathering in a harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crop' looks agricultural, which 'harvested' encourages, but it is a short haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: A very short, bristly haircut is what a close crop of the hair produces.

clue.text: Expert marksmanship of a certain kind

definitions.meaning: shooting that never misses, read literally
guaranteed, bound to succeed

explanation.surface: A particular style of skilled shooting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Certain' looks like 'particular' but means guaranteed.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally unerring shooting; idiomatically, infallible and bound to work.

clue.text: Suggested naughty child copied Matilda

parts.note: Belloc's cautionary-verse heroine told dreadful lies

explanation.surface: A badly behaved child imitated a girl called Matilda.
explanation.walkthrough: Hilaire Belloc's cautionary poem 'Matilda, Who told Lies, and was Burned to Death' supplies the allusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Hinted at without stating outright, so conveyed indirectly.

clue.text: Famous orator — one who freezes in company?

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

explanation.surface: A great speaker who chills others in a group.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman statesman Marcus Tullius was Rome's greatest public speaker.

clue.text: Village of Gotham, or London borough

definitions.meaning: a neighbourhood of New York, nicknamed Gotham
a riverside district of south-east London, home of the meridian

explanation.surface: A place that could be either in New York or in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Gotham is a nickname for New York City, whose Lower Manhattan has Greenwich Village. The same name is a London borough on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A Manhattan neighbourhood (with 'Village') and a south-east London borough, famous for its observatory, share one name.

clue.text: Something that'll do for head, and point

definitions.meaning: a headland, a high promontory on the coast
a projecting piece of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: An item that serves as headgear, and its tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' tempts as the top of the body, but it means a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a headland and a point are coastal promontories, so one name covers both.

clue.text: English novelist appears in spots on TV

definitions.meaning: C. P. ..., author of the Strangers and Brothers sequence
white speckled interference on a television picture

explanation.surface: A British writer turns up on television adverts.
explanation.walkthrough: C. P. Snow wrote the Strangers and Brothers novels; 'spots' is the speckled interference on an old analogue picture, not adverts.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the author of The Masters, and the dotted interference on a badly tuned screen.

clue.text: Alternate courses for food

definitions.meaning: zigzag sailing courses into the wind
foodstuff, as in hard ... (ship's biscuit)

explanation.surface: Switching dishes back and forth at a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' suggests meals but is a sailing term; the food sense is ship's biscuit (hardtack) or slang for grub.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing manoeuvre zigzagging into the wind, and an old word for foodstuff, especially ship's biscuit.

clue.text: Firmness of purpose seen in: decision

definitions.meaning: determination, resolve
a formal ruling, such as a motion passed by a meeting

explanation.surface: Determination shown in a judgement.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from 'resolve': a firm will, and a formal decision voted on by an assembly.

clue.text: Indeed, a table contains these

indicators.note: contains signals that the letters sit inside the words indeed, a table

explanation.surface: A table certainly holds information.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'indeeD A TAble', and a table is exactly where such facts are laid out.
explanation.definitionFit: Facts and figures held in rows and columns are information collected for reference.

clue.text: How far does new order indicate what's ahead?

indicators.note: new order means the letters of how far does are put into a new sequence

explanation.surface: How far does a new system hint at the future?
explanation.definitionFit: To give an advance sign or warning of a future event; a prefigure.
